results.answer:
It mostly makes things worse for using the injected context.

- On standard factuality benchmarks, some enhancement methods do improve performance. In Table 1, LLaMA2-7B-Chat’s TruthfulQA scores rise from **37.6 / 54.6 / 28.1** (MC1/MC2/MC3) for the baseline to **54.2 / 73.9 / 44.3** with **TruthX**, and to **46.3 / 69.1 / 41.2** with **ICD** (P5_0).
- But when the task is to follow injected context that conflicts with parametric knowledge, the same methods hurt badly. In Table 2, every evaluated method drops below the baseline on MQuAKE for both models (P6_2). For example, on **LLaMA2-7B-Chat** the baseline gets **68.5 / 78.7 / 81.3 / 82.5** across 3-shot/5-shot/10-shot/COT, while **TruthX** falls to **26.7 / 32.5 / 32.7 / 26.5** and **ICD** to **50.1 / 61.7 / 64.9 / 60.5** (P6_2).
- The paper summarizes this trade-off as a large drop in context-faithfulness despite gains in factuality, with **TruthX** showing a **-61.1%** change in context-faithfulness in Figure 3 (P6_2).
- Mechanistically, Figure 4 shows why: after injection, **new-knowledge tokens get lower average logits while parametric-knowledge tokens get higher**. For LLaMA2-7B-Chat, the baseline has **47.21** vs **13.63** (new vs parametric), but **TruthX** reverses this to **15.67** vs **25.75** (P7_0). The text states this explains the reduced context-faithfulness (P7_0).

So the answer is: **yes, it can cause the model to reject the correct injected information instead of improving accuracy**. The paper’s overall claim is that these methods “significantly reduce the accuracy of knowledge editing tasks” and undermine context-faithfulness, even though they may improve factuality elsewhere (P7_1).</answer

results.answer:
Not fully. In this paper, the self-supervised depth–normal consistency loss \(L_c\) is helpful, but it does not by itself solve sharp-feature reconstruction.

Evidence:
- The authors explicitly state on **P7_0** that “**the self-supervised consistency loss alone does not guarantee correct surface**” and that errors remain “**especially near depth discontinuities**.”
- On **P7_1**, ablation shows \(L_c\) improves overall geometry substantially: removing it worsens average **Chamfer distance from 0.882 to 1.243** and lowers **PSNR from 32.51 to 31.56**. So it does help reduce artifacts in general.
- But for fine sharp geometry, other terms matter more. The same page (**P7_1**) says that with opacity loss \(L_o\), the **“LEGO studs are better reconstructed, with sharper edges.”** It also notes that the normal-prior loss can help geometric accuracy in highlighted areas.

So the verdict is: **\(L_c\) improves reconstruction and reduces some artifacts, but it does not on its own reliably preserve sharp edges/corners.** For those fine geometric features, the paper shows you still need additional terms—especially **opacity loss**, and sometimes **normal-prior loss**—to get truly sharp detail.

results.answer:
No. In the infinite-data limit, knowing the observation operator and temperature does **not** guarantee unique recovery of the true reward function \(R\).

From **P17_0**, the paper states:

- “In the infinite data limit, do the human choice probabilities \(P^R\) collectively provide enough information to uniquely identify the reward function \(R\)?”  
- **Proposition 3.1**: the choice probabilities determine the **return function** \(G\) **only “up to an additive constant.”**
- Immediately after, it says: **“The reward function \(R\) is not necessarily identifiable from preference comparisons; see Skalse et al. [2023, Lemma B.3] for a precise characterization.”**

So the best identifiability result visible here is that you can recover the return function \(G\) up to an additive constant, which is enough for the optimal policy since it is invariant under adding a constant to \(G\). But you cannot in general uniquely pin down the exact reward function \(R\) itself.

Moreover, under partial observability (**P18_2**), things can be worse: RLHF may infer an observation-based return \(G_{\text{obs}}\) rather than \(G\), and this inferred return “might … imply an incorrect set of optimal policies.”

No. Under a strict token budget, Tree-of-Thoughts (ToT) does **not** still beat Chain-of-Thought with self-consistency (CoT-SC) on math reasoning.

Evidence:

- On that task, the paper states plainly: **“The performance of Tree-of-Thoughts lags that of a simple SC by a considerable margin”** and that ToT needs a **“significant budget commitment”** to deliver its best performance (**P11_2**).
- In **Figure 5** on **P7_0**, for **GPT-4**, **CoT-SC (100 samples)** reaches about **0.55 accuracy** very quickly, while **ToT with beam widths 1, 3, 5** stays below that at low budgets and only approaches/roughly matches CoT-SC after spending far more tokens.
- The ablation on **P9_1** quantifies the cost issue on Game of 24:
  - **b=5, GPT-4 proposer + GPT-3.5 evaluator:** **$33.53** cost, **72%** accuracy.
  - **GPT-4 evaluator instead:** **$159.87** cost, only **76%** accuracy.

So the answer is: **no—under a strict token budget, CoT with self-consistency generally wins or at least beats ToT; ToT’s advantage only appears when you give it a much larger budget.**

And from **P5_2**, the paper says the **initial components** capture **rough direction and length**, while the **subsequent components** encode **high-frequency details like curliness**.

So adding more coefficients does **not** steadily improve global shape and fine details together. Instead:
- **Global shape** is already mostly captured by about **10** coefficients.
- **Additional coefficients** mainly refine **fine details** (curl patterns/high-frequency structure).

The paper also notes on **P6_0** that they use **64 coefficients total**, which explains **almost 100%** of the training-set variance, but the decomposition itself is not a uniform “more coefficients = better everything” story.</

results.answer:
No—not strictly for every model family.

On this paper’s NLL plot (Figure 3, page id **P2_1**), most families do keep dropping or flattening as shots increase:

- **Qwen1.5 4B:** about **1.67 → 1.45**
- **Qwen1.5 7B:** about **1.50 → 1.32**
- **Mistral 7B:** about **1.10 → 1.01**
- **Llama3 8B:** about **1.30 → 1.10**
- **Gemma 7B:** about **1.46 → 1.29**

But **Gemma 2B** breaks the “always lower” pattern: its NLL falls to about **1.66** at **32 shots**, then rises slightly to about **1.68** at **64 shots**. So the trend is not monotonic for that family.

This matches the authors’ own wording on **P2_0**: using NLL, they say there is a general decrease with more shots, but there are also “clear diminishing returns.” So the right conclusion is: **generally yes, but not uniformly all the way up across every model family.**

It does **not** keep climbing with more channels. In this paper, keeping **only the low-frequency DCT components is better**, and the sweet spot is around **64 channels**.

From **Table 3 on page P1_2**:

- **CIFAR-10:**  
  - 6 channels: **89.7 ± 0.6%**  
  - 24 channels: **91.2 ± 0.6%**  
  - 48 channels: **91.7 ± 0.6%**  
  - 64 channels: **92.4 ± 0.6%**  
  - 192 channels: **92.3 ± 0.6%**

- **mini-ImageNet:**  
  - 6 → 24 → 48 → 64 → 192 channels:  
    **81.6 → 90.0 → 90.1 → 89.5 → 89.7** (all ±1.8%)

- **Imagenette:**  
  - **84.3 → 87.5 → 86.4 → 86.5 → 83.8** (all ±0.4%)

- **ImageNet:**  
  - **55.5 → 65.8 → 66.1 → 66.3 → 64.1** (all ±1.0%)

The text right below Table 3 on **P1_2** explicitly says: **“retaining the top 64 low-frequency channels yielded the best accuracy”** and that the full **192-channel lossless representation contains unnecessary high-frequency components that hinder learning**.

So the answer is: **accuracy improves as you add low-frequency DCT channels, but then plateaus or drops once you include too many high-frequency ones; keeping mainly the low-frequency channels is better.**

Accuracy is **not** monotonic. In Figure 2, the paper shows that adding more fine-tuned layers often helps at first, but then performance can drop again once you pass an optimal point (P4_0). - **RACE-mid**: rises to **83.77**, then drops to **82.19** before ending at **82.86**.
- **RACE-high**: peaks at **81.22**, then declines to **80.99**.

So the sweep shows **clear reversals**, not a steady “more layers = better accuracy” trend.

results.answer:
It’s the latter in this paper: **VPT is the raw forecast horizon where the error first exceeds a threshold**, not a definition that divides by the maximum Lyapunov exponent.

Specifically, on **P2_0** the paper states:
- **“Valid Prediction Time (VPT). The first forecast horizon at which the sMAPE exceeds a fixed threshold ε.”**
- And gives  
  **VPT = argmax_{t_f} { t_f | sMAPE(x_t, x̂_t) < ε, ∀ t < t_f }**.

Then on **P2_1** it says:
- **“We set ε = 30.”**

The Lyapunov exponent/time enters differently. On **P3_2**, the paper says each system is annotated with its largest Lyapunov exponent **λ**, and defines the **Lyapunov time** as **τ ≡ λ⁻¹**. It also says the dataset is aligned to these dominant timescales and sampled at **30 timepoints per Lyapunov time τ**. So Lyapunov time is used for **normalizing/aligning the benchmark and reporting**, while **VPT itself is still defined by the threshold-crossing horizon**.

Figure 3 caption on **P2_2** reinforces this: VPT is “the first time each forecast exceeds an error limit.”

results.answer:
Not threshold balancing alone — you need **delayed evaluation** on top of it.

Specifically, the paper’s ablation shows that **channel-wise local threshold balancing (CLTB)** helps, but the gains are best preserved only when combined with **delayed evaluation (CLTB+DE)**: the output is computed as the **average spike count in the last layer from a delayed start step \(t_0\) to \(T\)**, instead of averaging over all time steps (P6_0). The ablation plot labels this as **CLTB+DE**, and the text says the full pipeline “consistently outperforms … across all time-steps,” especially with delayed evaluation (P5_1, P5_0).

In UniVoxel’s own ablation over illumination representations built on its voxelization framework, the SG-based method is the best for albedo. In Table 2, **SG (16 lobes)** gets **29.933 Albedo PSNR**, beating:

However, in the full comparison against other inverse-rendering baselines on the MII synthetic set, **UniVoxel is not the absolute top on raw albedo PSNR**:

No.

From the retrieved pages, **local rank** is defined purely as a **descriptive quantity**, not a regularization term added to prevent divergence. Specifically, on **P12_0**, Definition 1 says:

\[
\text{LR}_l=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim \text{Data}}[\text{rank}(J_x p_l)]
\]

So it is the **expected Jacobian rank** at a layer—i.e., a measure of representation dimensionality, not a penalty or stabilizer.

Separately, the paper’s **scaling/stability** notion is about keeping activations/features bounded as width grows, not about using local rank as a regularizer. On **P16_0/P16_1**, Definition 3 says LoRA finetuning is stable if

\[
Z,\;Z_A,\;Z_B = \mathcal{O}(1)\quad\text{as }n\to\infty
\]

and explicitly states this means **“no quantity in the network explodes as width grows.”** That is the anti-divergence condition there.

Also, in the basic LoRA formulation on **P17_1**, the rank \(r\) appears only inside the low-rank update structure:

\[
W' = W_0 + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA
\]

It does **not** appear as a regularization factor whose purpose is to prevent divergence.

So the short answer is: **No—local rank itself is not incorporated as a regularization factor for preventing divergence. The anti-divergence behavior comes from stability/scaling conditions like \(Z,Z_A,Z_B=\mathcal{O}(1)\), while local rank is just a measured property of the learned representations.**

- **CATENet** (deep neural network)
- **TabPFN** (DR-learner + foundation model)

The caption/text says that **“both methods effectively controlled the type-1 error, except for LOCO when CATENet is used”** (**P10_0**).

- **CF:** about **0.02**
- **CATENet:** about **0.02**
- **TabPFN:** about **0.03**

So the answer is:

- **No, it does not strictly control Type-I error identically across all meta-learner architectures.**
- **But in this experiment, it does keep Type-I error below the 0.05 target for all three architectures**, unlike the compared method LOCO, which inflates to about **0.07** with CATENet.

results.answer:
Yes. The reviewed papers say you do **not** need to abandon the standard GNN message-passing style.

- **P0_0**: A topological neural network (TNN) is described as being **“like a GNN”**—stacked layers that transform data using **neighborhoods and message passing**.
- **P3_2**: It breaks message passing into just **four steps**:
  1. **Message** from neighbor \(y\) to \(x\),
  2. **Within-neighborhood aggregation**,
  3. **Between-neighborhood aggregation**,
  4. **Update** of the cell feature.  
  In the **simplest case**, the message step is just a **neighborhood matrix** \(M\) propagating features:
  \[
  m^{(r'\!\to r)}_{y\to x}=M_{xy}\,h_y^{t,(r')}\,\Theta^t
  \]
  So it is still local linear message passing + aggregation + update.

- **P3_0** adds that in the **standard convolutional** setting, each incoming message is simply multiplied by a **learned scalar**; more complex attention/general schemes are optional extensions.

So the answer is: **yes, you can move to topological/multi-way domains while staying close to standard GNN simplicity**. The extra structure mainly changes **which neighborhood structures** are used and how they are aggregated; the core layer operation remains message passing over a neighborhood, not necessarily heavy algebraic-topology machinery.

Evidence:

  - **Random sampling**: sample nonexistent objects randomly

- **P9_1** explicitly states: *“the performance of LVLMS consistently decreases, from **random** settings, to **popular** and **adversarial**.”*

results.answer:
It applies updates to a single shared state vector, not separate branch-wise covariances.

Evidence:
- The overview says there are two branches—an event module and an image module—and “Both module predictions are fed into the Kalman filter” (P9_1).
- The paper then defines one state vector and one covariance matrix: \(x=(x,y,v_x,v_y)^T\) and \(P\) (P9_2).
- It explicitly says that when a measurement arrives, the Kalman filter updates “the internal state and uncertainty,” incorporating \(\Delta\hat p\) and \(\Sigma\) from “our event or image module” (P9_2).
- The update step is given in standard Kalman form with a single state/covariance pair: \(\hat x_{k|k}, P_{k|k}\) updated from \(\hat x_{k|k-1}, P_{k|k-1}\) and the new measurement \(z_k\) (P9_2, P8_2).

So the answer is: it uses a single shared state vector/covariance updated by branch measurements, rather than coupling branches through separate/joint covariances.</

results.answer:
No. In this paper, the demand-query advantage is mainly an early-round phenomenon, not a lasting one.

- On page **P2_1**, the authors explicitly say **“DQs Offer Superior Efficiency Gains in Initial Rounds,”** but immediately follow with **“VQs Offer Superior Efficiency Gains in Later Rounds.”**
- The same page (**P2_1**) states that for any ε > 0, there are infinitely many auction instances where **no combination of DQs can achieve efficiency above 50% + ε**. It also says a **single DQ can cause an efficiency drop arbitrarily close to 100%**.
- By contrast, page **P2_0** says **VQ-based auctions can always achieve 100% efficiency after sufficiently many VQs**, and adding more VQs **never reduces efficiency**.

So the DQ edge does **not** persist into later rounds; instead, it fades and can even hurt, while VQs become more powerful later.

Not reliably. The paper says that in multi-label backdoor settings, non-cooperative attackers often “exclude each other”: they compete for neuron weights, and “the dominant attacker controls most neurons … resulting in others failing to achieve their backdoor function” (P13_2).

So empirically, the attacks do not usually stay equally strong together. In the lifespan experiment, baseline methods fall quickly because of this exclusion, while only Mirage and A3FL keep ASRs above 90% at the end (P11_0).

The table also shows this imbalance explicitly via the GAP metric (difference between highest and lowest attacker ASR): with no defense on CIFAR-10,
- Vanilla: mean ASR 31.88%, GAP 87.68
- PGD: 31.25%, GAP 92.78
- Neurotoxin: 52.99%, GAP 90.29
- Chameleon: 39.65%, GAP 79.98  
(P12_0)

By contrast, Mirage keeps all attackers much more balanced:
- CIFAR-10: 99.54% ASR, GAP 0.27
- CIFAR-100: 99.05%, GAP 0.77
- GTSRB: 99.73%, GAP 0.48  
(P12_0)

So the answer is: generally, one attack tends to dominate while the others weaken, unless a method specifically mitigates this exclusion.

Yes. The paper reports that reasoning benchmarks are more robust than language-understanding benchmarks when later attention blocks are bypassed.

Evidence:

- The accompanying text on **P5_0** says the **average relative score decrease** for reasoning tasks (**PIQA, ARC-Easy**) is **“much lesser”** than for language-understanding tasks (**Hellaswag, LAMBADA**), and some transformer blocks show **“almost zero drop”** on reasoning tasks after short-circuiting.
- For Pythia models, **P3_1** (Fig. 3) says short-circuiting later blocks reduces memorization with a **“negligible drop in downstream benchmark performance on PIQA.”**
- For GPTNeo-1.3B, **P4_0/P7_0** notes that short-circuiting the last quartile blocks—**layers 18–24**—gives a big memorization reduction with **“negligible drop in model performance,”** and in some cases the short-circuited model even outperforms the original on **LAMBADA**.

So the answer is **yes**: reasoning tasks generally hold up better than non-reasoning tasks when later attention layers are short-circuited.

No. In this paper, iterative methods do **not** reliably beat standard CoT once the compute budget gets large.

- The figure captions reinforce this:
  - **Figure 1**: “As increasing the sample time \(N\), the accuracy of CoT grows rapidly and it dominates on all models when \(N\) is large enough.” (**P4_0**)
  - **Figure 2**: “Under the equal cost \(O\), CoT performs best most of the time. When \(O\) grows larger, CoT gradually becomes the best prompt strategy \(P_O^*\) on all models.” (**P4_0**)

So the answer is: **no—at large test-time compute, simple CoT usually beats the iterative prompting strategies, not the other way around.**

results.answer:
It does something more complicated than “more steps = smaller error.”

- The paper’s general bound is explicitly described as a **trade-off**: in Theorem 2, adding more sampling steps makes one part of the bound **accumulate** while another part **shrinks**. Specifically, on **P0_1**, the text says that with more steps,  
  \[
  \frac{\alpha_{t_1}^2}{4\sigma_{t_1}^2}R^2+\sum_{j=2}^N \frac{\alpha_{t_j}^2}{4\sigma_{t_j}^2}t_{j-1}^2\frac{\epsilon_{\mathrm{cm}}^2}{\Delta\tau^2}
  \]
  accumulates, whereas the term \(t_N\frac{\epsilon_{\mathrm{cm}}}{\Delta\tau}\) decreases because \(t_N\) becomes shorter.

- In the OU/variance-preserving case study, this means going from **1 step to 2 steps** can help, but **further gains are not guaranteed**. On **P2_0**, Corollary 1 shows the 2-step bound is better than the 1-step bound, and the text says: **“further improvement with this heuristic is challenging.”**

- In the variance-exploding case study, the trade-off is even clearer: on **P2_1**, the paper states that with more steps, **term (i) increases at a linear rate** while **term (ii) decreases exponentially**. So the overall bound does **not** just keep dropping monotonically; it balances an accumulating component against a shrinking one.

So the short answer is: **no**—the theoretical bound does not simply keep decreasing with more steps; it exhibits a **trade-off/accumulation vs reduction** behavior.

It falls off rather than keeping rising.

On page **P6_2**, the paper defines **learnability** as  
\[
p(1-p)
\]
where \(p\) is the fraction of times the agent solves the level. This means the “utility” combines two things:

- **\(p\)**: chance of getting positive learning experience from the level, and  
- **\(1-p\)**: remaining room for improvement.

So the expected improvement is **not monotonic in success rate**.

This is also visible in **Figure 2(c) on P7_0 / P6_1**: the learnability score rises from very low values at low success rates, peaks around a **mean success rate of about 0.5–0.6**, and then drops back toward **~0 by about 0.9 success rate**.

So the answer is: **it rises only up to a point, then falls off once the task becomes too easy.**

So under severe distribution shift, whether TTA still beats a zero-shot baseline depends mainly on how good the adapted model already is before adaptation — especially its **source-domain/OOD accuracy, feature properties, and classifier quality**.

In the retrieved paper, the authors created “stitched” documents by concatenating short, unrelated documents (fewer than 10 sentences each) into longer texts averaging about 100 sentences (P15_2). They then compared chunkers using document retrieval F1@5 (P15_2).

From Table 1 on P16_0:

- On the stitched datasets (*), the best results were mixed:
  - Miracl*: 81.89 (Breakpoint)
  - NQ*: 63.93 (Breakpoint)
  - Scidocs*: 19.87 (Clustering)
  - Scifact*: 36.27 (Breakpoint)
  - BioASQ*: 62.49 (Clustering)
  - NFCorpus*: 22.12 (Clustering)

- On the non-stitched datasets, fixed-size/isolated-segment chunking was usually strongest:
  - HotpotQA: 90.59 (Fixed-size)
  - MSMARCO: 93.58 (Fixed-size)
  - ConditionalQA: 68.11 (Fixed-size)
  - Qasper: 90.99 (Fixed-size)

The paper also states that semantic chunking “occasionally improved performance, particularly on stitched datasets with high topic diversity,” but those gains were “highly context-dependent” and did not consistently justify the extra cost; on non-synthetic datasets, fixed-size chunking often performed better (P16_0).

So the answer is: no, training/evaluating on artificially concatenated unrelated chunks does not reliably improve retrieval accuracy versus working with more isolated/original segments; if anything, isolated-segment/fixed-size chunking tends to perform better on real-like data.

results.answer:
No—at least in the formulations I found, it does **not** reduce to a simple scalar multiplication of text and vision similarities.

- On **P18_1**, the paper defines a **Text Image Residual Gating** operator as  
  \[
  \phi_{xt}^{rg}=w_g f_{gate}(\phi_x,\phi_t)+w_r f_{res}(\phi_x,\phi_t)
  \]
  with  
  \[
  f_{gate}(\phi_x,\phi_t)=\sigma(W_{g2}*\mathrm{ReLU}(W_{g1}*[ \phi_x,\phi_t ]))\odot \phi_x .
  \]
  So the “gate” there is a learned transformation plus **element-wise product** (\(\odot\)), not a simple \(sim_{text}\times sim_{vision}\) combination.

- In another retrieved formulation on **P18_0**, the multimodal fusion is written as  
  \[
  H = H_{\text{text}}+\Lambda \,\mathrm{Embed}_{\text{image}}(z),
  \]
  where \(\Lambda=\mathrm{sigmoid}(W_\Lambda \mathrm{Embed}_{\text{image}}(z)+U_\Lambda H_{\text{text}})\). That is **additive gated fusion**, again not a simple multiplicative similarity gate.

So based on the visible equations, the answer is **no**: the retrieved multimodal late-fusion operators are **more structured than a plain multiplicative similarity gate**.

results.answer:
Yes. On page **P1_0**, the paper defines a potential-based shaping term using the teacher’s state-value function:

\[
\psi(s_t, a_t)=V_\phi(s_{t+1})-V_\phi(s_t)
\]

and then incorporates it directly into the policy objective:

\[
\max_{\pi_\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(s,a)\sim \pi_\theta}\big[r(s,a)+\alpha \psi_\phi(s,a)\big]
\]

This leads to the final TVKD loss, Eq. (3), where the shaping term appears explicitly in the exponentiated reward terms for the chosen/rejected examples:

\[
L_{\mathrm{TVKD}}(\pi_\theta,\mathcal D;\pi_\phi)=-\mathbb{E}_{(\tau_w,\tau_l)\sim \mathcal D}\!\left[\log \sigma\!\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(a^w\mid s^w)}{\exp\!\big(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\psi_\phi(s^w,a^w)\big)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(a^l\mid s^l)}{\exp\!\big(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\psi_\phi(s^l,a^l)\big)}\right)\right]
\]

So the core objective **does** mathematically incorporate the token-level transition difference of the teacher’s value function as a potential-based reward-shaping term (**P1_0**).</

Not consistently. In the retrieved multi-label imbalance results, the balancing loss **DB** improves **total micro-F1**, but not **total macro-F1** across both datasets (Table 2, **P13_0**; method defined on **P14_0**):

- **Reuters-21578**: DB gets **90.62 / 64.47** micro/macro-F1 vs. **89.45 / 57.98** for DB-0FL, so it helps overall.
- **PubMed**: DB gets **48.89 / 31.39** micro/macro-F1, which is better than DB-0FL’s **58.95 / 15.15** in micro-F1, but its macro-F1 is still below **CB-NTR**’s **61.07 / 18.40**.

So the verdict is: **it improves overall F1 only partially — yes for micro-F1, but not reliably for macro-F1 on highly imbalanced data**.

The authors state directly: “the in-context learning approach increases input token overhead as JSON objects grow larger” (P2_2). They also note that this increase “could offset the cost savings” (P2_2).

- Claude: Full = 918 input tokens, Diff = 1,890 input tokens
- GPT-4o-mini: Full = 677 input tokens, Diff = 1,500 input tokens

So while the diff/edit method does reduce output tokens—Claude from 918 to 529, and 4o-mini from 677 to 464 (P3_0)—it uses more input tokens, not fewer.

results.answer:
Not reliably. In Table 3, the paper states that for this two-way classification task, chance accuracy is 50% (P6_0). On incomplete evidence (“Inc.”), the strong LLMs often fall below that baseline:

- EntailmentBank: all listed LLMs are below 50% — Llama3.1 8B 18.8%, 70B 26.5%, Claude3 Haiku 28.5%, Claude3 Sonnet 43.5%, Claude3.5 Sonnet 44.2%, GPT-4o 34.4% (P6_0).
- MuSiQue: only one model clears 50% — Llama3.1 70B at 51.6%; the others are 40.0%, 47.6%, 48.6%, 31.4%, and 48.0% (P6_0).

They do beat chance on some other incomplete-evidence splits:

- WiCE: mostly above 50% — 28.4%, 83.2%, 83.2%, 84.6%, 88.8%, 68.4% (P6_0).
- HotpotQA: all above 50% — 55.0%, 58.6%, 67.0%, 65.4%, 67.6%, 82.2% (P6_0).

So the short answer is: no, not consistently. On incomplete evidence, capable LLMs often fail to beat random, and on EntailmentBank they are all clearly worse than the 50% baseline (P6_0).

results.answer:
No—at least not in the form evaluated here.

From the retrieved L2D pages, candidate item representations are built by aggregating hidden states from training samples associated with each item (P10_0, P10_1). That means an item needs prior training interactions/mentions to have a usable latent representation. For a truly cold-start item with zero interaction history, there would be no such stored hidden-state pairs to aggregate.

Also, the paper’s experimental setup does not include a zero-interaction or unseen-item evaluation. The retrieved results page reports overall metrics on standard datasets (Amazon-Book, MovieLens, Yelp, Steam) but not a separate “unseen items” or “zero-interaction items” setting (P14_0).

So the best-supported conclusion from these pages is: latent-space decoding works well for warm or at-least-somewhat-seen items, but it does not demonstrably handle completely cold-start items with zero interaction history.

The training objective then uses **inter-MCR** contrastive losses \(L_{ttc}\) and \(L_{avc}\) to align the projected pairs \((\hat t^I,\hat t^A)\) and \((\hat v^I,\hat a^A)\), plus **intra-MCR** losses \(L_{tv}\) and \(L_{va}\) (P10_0, P5_1). The final objective is
\[
L = L_{inter} + \lambda L_{intra}
\]
(P5_1).

There is **no visible explicit loss term** that directly matches an original embedding with its own augmented version. Instead, the framework relies on **cross-modal / modality-gap contrastive losses** to keep semantically related embeddings close, rather than an explicit original-vs-augmented consistency/contrastive term.

Not reliably.

In the retrieved paper, adding sensitive persona attributes to interaction-based prompts does **not** consistently preserve minority/niche preferences. The authors explicitly summarize that **“intersectional attributes amplify fairness gaps”** (P12_0), and they give a concrete qualitative example: a **“Young Adult Female”** prompt in music can push the recommender toward trending pop artists, **“moving it away from niche, user-preferred indie bands”** (P7_0).

The quantitative results show the same pattern when comparing single attributes to intersectional ones:

- Under **true preference alignment** with **random sampling**, the unfairness metric **SNSV** is:
  - **Sex:** **0.0105**
  - **Age:** **0.0179**
  - **Intersectional (Sex & Age):** **0.0305**  
  (P11_1)

- And **SNSR** is:
  - **Sex:** **0.0210**
  - **Age:** **0.0226**
  - **Intersectional:** **0.0342**  
  (P11_1)

So, if “preserving minority opinions” means keeping recommendations aligned with users’ actual niche tastes, the evidence here says: **no, not automatically**. Persona+history prompting can help in some settings, but **more demographic signals often worsen disparities** and can suppress minority/niche preferences rather than protect them.

results.answer:
From a softmax over the raw continuous SNN output, not directly from spike history itself.

On page **P11_0**, the paper says the SNN’s outputs are **“accumulated spikes”** (or, in some cases, **“the membrane potential of integrate-but-not-fire neurons”**), and then states that confidence is obtained **“after applying Softmax to the SNN outputs.”** The formula shown there is:

\[
\hat{P}_t = \max_i \frac{e^{z_i^t}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j^t}}
\]

So the spike history / membrane potential produces the continuous logit vector \(z^t\), and confidence is judged from the **softmax over that raw output**.</answer

results.answer:
Not universally.

In the paper’s dense MAPF experiments, GNN/neural guidance still helps at high density, but the effect is scenario-dependent rather than absolute.

- On the **densest** maps in **Figure 6**, removing neural guidance (“w/o neural guidance,” i.e. reverting to plain LaCAM) clearly hurts solution quality (**P7_0**):
  - **Dense Warehouse:** SoC/lb rises from about **5.2** with LaGAT-init to about **17.0** without the model, while success drops from about **1.0** to **0.9**.
  - **Dense Room:** SoC/lb goes from about **4.8** to about **8.8**, with success staying near **1.0**.
  - **Dense Maze:** SoC/lb goes from about **4.0** to about **5.8**, with success near **1.0**.
  
  The authors summarize this by saying all components are essential and that neural guidance contributes significantly to reducing solution cost (**P7_0**).

- But the same paper also says the advantage **does not extend universally**: on larger, **sparser** maps like **ost003d**, the search baseline **lacam3** produces near-optimal solutions, while the GNN-guided method gives only slightly suboptimal initial solutions (**P5_0**).

So the right takeaway is: **yes, GNN guidance still provides a clear benefit in the dense/high-congestion regime, but it is not a blanket “always better” advantage once the density setting changes or the map becomes less constrained.**

results.answer:
To make degradation comparisons robust across tasks with very different baselines, do **not** use raw score differences or a fixed denominator. Instead, **normalize the loss relative to the meaningful performance range on that task**.

Two concrete formulations visible in the retrieved pages are:

- **Relative Performance Ratio (RPR)**: normalize the degraded score \(Q_i^d\) between an acceptance line \(Q_i^{ac}\) and an excellence line \(Q_i^{ex}\):
  \[
  RPR_i=\sigma\!\left(\frac{Q_i^d-Q_i^{ac}}{Q_i^{ex}-Q_i^{ac}}\right)
  \]
  This keeps comparisons on a common scale; the paper notes \(RPR_i>0.5\) means above the acceptance line and \(RPR_i>0.73\) (\(\sigma(1)\)) means above the excellence line.  
  Source: **P19_1 / P19_2**.

- **Degradation percentage normalized by the effective range**:
  \[
  \text{Degradation \%}=\frac{\max\bigl(GT-\max(\text{AVG},\text{ZERO},\text{RANDOM}),0\bigr)}{GT-\min(\text{AVG},\text{ZERO},\text{RANDOM})}\times 100\%
  \]
  Here the numerator measures the drop below the best trivial baseline, and the denominator scales it by the full usable gap between ground truth and the worst trivial baseline.  
  Source: **P18_2**.

So the robust principle is: **measure degradation as a fraction of the task’s usable performance span**, not as an absolute change from one baseline.

The retrieved evidence says this is not consistent. On **P19_0** (Fig. 1), the paper states that an intrinsic-reward method **“does not consistently outperform a method trained using only extrinsic rewards”** across Atari games. It helps in some sparse-reward settings like **Montezuma’s Revenge**, but it **“hurts in other games such as James Bond.”** In Fig. 1b on **P19_0**, the **Extrinsic + Intrinsic** curve is clearly **above Extrinsic-only in Montezuma’s Revenge**, but **below Extrinsic-only in James Bond**.

The same idea appears on **P19_1**: in the 2D navigation example, **RND gets distracted by intrinsic rewards** and **“performs worse than the agent that optimizes only the extrinsic reward (EO).”**

So the verdict is: **No—agents with auxiliary internal/intrinsic rewards do not consistently outperform sparse external-feedback-only agents during the initial stages of learning; the effect is task-dependent.**

results.answer:
No—not universally.

From the retrieved pages:

- **Standard non-equivariant PEFT baselines underperform.** On **rMD17-Aspirin**, the ablation compares **Full FT**, **ELoRA**, **MMEA**, **Readout**, and **Adapter**. The non-equivariant baselines are much worse than both full FT and the equivariant PEFT methods:
  - **Full:** **9.7** energy / **23.9** forces
  - **ELoRA:** **8.0** / **18.3**
  - **MMEA:** **7.3** / **16.4**
  - **Readout:** **23.8** / **36.8**
  - **Adapter:** **11.0** / **26.3**  
  (Tables 6 / P9_0 and P11_1)

  The paper also states that these standard strategies “**underperform full fine-tuning, ELoRA, and MMEA**” because they break equivariance (P9_0).

- **Equivariant PEFT can beat full fine-tuning on some OOD generalization tasks.** For example:
  - **3BPA at 600 K:** **Full 6.5 / 15.5** vs **MMEA 6.5 / 15.4**
  - **3BPA at 1200 K:** **Full 17.6 / 42.0** vs **MMEA 17.1 / 39.7**
  - **AcAc at 600 K:** **Full 3.9 / 13.6** vs **MMEA(r=32) 3.2 / 13.0**  
  (Table 3 and Table 4, P9_0)

- **But under extreme OOD, full fine-tuning wins.** In the **MACE-MP inorganic→organic** transfer benchmark, full FT beats both equivariant PEFT methods:
  - **Aspirin:** **Full 11.4 / 29.4** vs **ELoRA 12.5 / 31.1** vs **MMEA 13.3 / 31.9**
  - **Uracil:** **Full 3.4 / 19.7** vs **ELoRA 3.5 / 20.7** vs **MMEA 3.6 / 21.4**  
  (Table 7, P11_1)

  The paper explicitly summarizes this regime: **“when the distribution gap … is large, one should train from scratch or perform full fine-tuning”** (P11_1).

So the overall answer is: **equivariant PEFT methods clearly outperform standard non-equivariant PEFT baselines, and they can outperform full fine-tuning on some OOD tasks, but they do not consistently beat full fine-tuning on all OOD prediction tasks—especially under large distribution shifts.**

In this paper’s comparison, the gradient-based approximation is **Gradient × Input (GxI)** and the perturbation-based estimator is **LIME** (P5_2). GxI only beats LIME in **LSTM** settings, not in **BERT**.

From the precision tables:

- **LSTM**
  - **Ordered-pair precision**: GxI is higher on all three datasets  
    - **SST2:** 0.92 vs 0.85  
    - **IMDB:** 0.81 vs 0.80  
    - **Toxicity:** 0.88 vs 0.66  
    (P3_0 vs P2_0)
  - **Single-token precision**: GxI ties or slightly exceeds LIME  
    - **SST2:** 1.00 vs 1.00  
    - **IMDB:** 1.00 vs 0.99–1.00  
    - **Toxicity:** 1.00 vs 1.00  
    (P3_0 vs P2_0)
  - **Token-in-context precision**: GxI is worse on all three datasets  
    - **SST2:** 0.76 vs 0.83–0.84  
    - **IMDB:** 0.35 vs 0.78–0.66  
    - **Toxicity:** 0.68 vs 0.84–0.85  
    (P3_0 vs P2_0)

- **BERT**
  - GxI **does not outperform** LIME on any shown precision metric. LIME is higher across all datasets and shortcut types; e.g.

    - **IMDB tic:** 0.98 vs 0.35  
    - **Toxicity op:** 0.78 vs 0.47  
    (P3_0 vs P2_0)

So the answer is: **the gradient-based approximation outperforms the perturbation-based method mainly for LSTM models on ordered-pair precision, and it ties or marginally beats LIME on single-token precision; it does not win on BERT.**

results.answer:
It is implemented as a **joint regularization penalty**, not an explicit asymmetric projection of the forgetting gradient.

On **P6_1**, the paper defines:

- \(g_f = \nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[L_{\text{forget}}]\)
- \(g_r = \nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}[L_{\text{retain}}]\)

and then adds the **AO regularization term**

\[
\mathcal{R}_{AO}=\mathbb{I}(g_f\cdot g_r<0)\left(\frac{1-\cos(g_f,g_r)}{2}\right)^{\gamma}
\]

to the unified objective

\[
L_{\text{unlearn}} = L_{\text{forget}}(h_f) + L_{\text{retain}}(h_r) + \lambda_{ao}\mathcal{R}_{AO}.
\]

So the orthogonality is enforced by **penalizing non-orthogonal alignment between forget and retain gradients** in the loss, rather than by projecting one gradient onto the other. The page also notes that when \(g_f\cdot g_r \ge 0\) (aligned/orthogonal case), the penalty is zero (**P6_1**).

And on **P6_2**, the authors explicitly contrast this with methods like **PGU**, which rely on “rigid, computationally expensive orthogonal projections,” whereas their method uses a “soft orthogonal constraint.”

results.answer:
Not reliably. The “same active parameters → same energy per token” idea works only in a narrow benchmark setting, not as a general rule across deployment scales.

Evidence:

- In **TokenPowerBench**, the authors explicitly say **“Mixtral-8×7B consumes roughly the same energy per token as a dense 8B model”** under their **single-node, 4 H100 GPU** setup (page **P11_2**).
- Their **Figure 3** also shows **Mixtral-8x7B’s total and GPU energy/token** are visually very close to **Llama3-8B** across context-length ranges (**P12_1**).

But that does **not** generalize cleanly:

- A separate study says sparse MoE can still be more expensive even with similar active compute. It reports that **OLMoE uses up to 54.24% more energy than OLMo-1B**, despite having a **“similar number of active parameters”** (**P13_0**).
- The same page attributes this to MoE overhead: the fused expert kernel is **19.70% slower at batch size 1** and **63% slower at batch size 8** than the dense GEMM counterpart (**P13_0**).
- Their **Figure 4** caption states the energy gap is **“pronounced at larger batch sizes”** (**P13_1**).
- Another paper explains why: MoE sparsity can reduce the effective FFN workload per device, leading to **lower GPU utilization during decoding** (**P11_0**).

So the answer is:

- **Yes, approximately, in some controlled setups** — e.g., TokenPowerBench’s 4-H100 evaluation makes Mixtral-8x7B look close to an 8B dense model.
- **No, not as a robust cross-scale rule** — depending on batch size, kernel implementation, and hardware utilization, a sparse MoE can consume **significantly more energy per token** than a dense model with similar active parameters.

So the answer is: vanilla GRPO tends to lose exploration over time; its policy entropy decays rapidly as training advances. Sustained exploration appears to require additional stabilization like Clip-Higher.

results.answer:
They use a combined hyperbolic hierarchy loss made of two parts:

- **Hyperbolic clustering loss** (\(L_{\text{cluster}}\), Eq. 3 on **P6_0**): a triplet-style loss over \((e, e^+, e^-)\) where \(e^+\) is a parent and \(e^-\) is a negative parent, forcing related entities to be closer in hyperbolic distance than unrelated ones:
  \[
  L_{\text{cluster}}=\sum_{(e,e^+,e^-)\in\mathcal D}\max(d_c(e,e^+)-d_c(e,e^-)+\alpha,0)
  \]

- **Hyperbolic centripetal loss** (\(L_{\text{centri}}\), Eq. 4 on **P6_0**): pushes parents closer to the Poincaré origin than their children, so that more general/hierarchical ancestors sit nearer the center:
  \[
  L_{\text{centri}}=\sum_{(e,e^+,e^-)\in\mathcal D}\max(\|e^+\|_c-\|e\|_c+\beta,0)
  \]

These are combined as the overall hierarchy re-training loss
\[
L_{\mathrm{Ht}} = L_{\text{cluster}} + L_{\text{centri}}
\]
(Eq. 5, **P6_0**). The paper notes that explicit hierarchies can come from structured sources like **taxonomies/ontologies** (**P7_2**), and that in hyperbolic space “distances increase exponentially relative to Euclidean distances as one moves from the origin to the boundary” (**P6_0**).

results.answer:
It depends on what you mean by “iterative self-refinement.”

- In the paper’s direct Yoruba→English self-refine test, the frontier models did **not** get measurably better in translation quality. On page **P5_1**, it says all three frontier LLMs “**have not received measurable improvements via the self-refine pipeline**,” and section 4.3 states self-refinement can improve **fluency and understandability but not quality**. The same page also says that for GPT-4/Gemini, “**actual performance does not improve through iterations**” even though their own self-scores do.

- But if you mean an **iterative refinement system applied to frontier LLMs** for standard MT, then **yes, it can hurt accuracy**. On page **P5_2** (Table 6), the iterative system **TransAgents** is worse than **GPT-4-Turbo**:
  - **En-Zh:** d-BLEU **29.3 vs 42.7**, COMETKiwi **75.5 vs 79.3**
  - **En-De:** d-BLEU **24.0 vs 25.5**, COMETKiwi **72.4 vs 70.5**

So the verdict is:
- **Pure self-refinement on frontier LLMs:** mostly **no clear accuracy gain**; often just neutral or misleadingly positive self-evaluation.
- **Iterative refinement systems built around frontier LLMs:** **yes, they can reduce translation accuracy**, as shown in Table 6 (**P5_2**).

results.answer:
No—not as much as one might expect from heavy shallow-layer pruning.

Under the proposed TENP method, the paper says it **“preserves the complete routing structure, allowing even pruned experts to remain routable”** (Figure 1, **P1_0/P2_1**). In other words, the router-to-expert graph is kept intact; what changes is mainly the internal neuron capacity of experts, not which experts exist or can be routed to.

The routing analysis on **P2_0** supports this:
- They compare expert selection frequencies for the full model, an expert-pruned baseline (**EASY_EP**), and **TENP**.
- The **“TENP - Full” difference heatmap** is visually much closer to zero than **“EASY_EP - Full.”**
- The text explicitly contrasts this with subset-based expert pruning, saying that when only a subset of experts is retained, it induces **“substantial changes in expert selection patterns,”** whereas TENP is designed to avoid that disruption.

So the verdict is: **the routing structure is largely preserved under TENP, despite the trapezoidal, depth-dependent pruning.** There may still be minor residual changes in how often individual experts are selected, but those changes are **much smaller** than the drastic shifts seen with methods that remove entire experts.

- **Table 4** on **P1_0** reports the EN–ZH / EN-docs ΔnDCG@10 as:
  - **E5:** **-0.018**
  - **GTE:** **-0.054**
  - **Jina:** **-0.147**
  - **Qwen3-0.6B:** **+0.006**
  - **Qwen3-8B:** **+0.053**
  
So there are a couple of tiny positive deltas for some Qwen3 models, but they are small and mixed in sign.

The paper’s overall conclusion matches that pattern: **P2_1** says for **EN-only documents, the optimum is usually unmixed** (`λ* = 0` in **8/13** cases), and **P1_0** says any occasional positive values on English-document settings are still much smaller than the gains seen on non-English documents.

So the short answer is: **No—there is no clear genuine retrieval gain from adding Chinese to English queries on English document indices; at best, there are only tiny, inconsistent bumps for a few models.**

results.answer:
No. In this study, successful human persuaders rely much more on **knowledge** than on **trust**, while the LLMs do the opposite.

- For human opinion-changing comments (Δ), the paper says they are more likely to convey **knowledge (84%)** and **similarity (58%)** than non-opinion-changing comments, while **trust is the second-least frequent dimension** in those successful human comments (P5_0).
- By contrast, “**all three LLMs overwhelmingly express trust**,” with “**nearly all generated messages incorporating this dimension**” (P5_0).
- Compared with successful human Δ comments, the models are **far more likely to express trust**, but **less likely to convey similarity and knowledge by 39% and 47%** (P5_0).
- The odds ratios in Figure 3 make this even sharper:  
  - **Trust vs. Δ**: **375.31** (Llama2-7B), **434.93** (Mistral-7B), **611.28** (GPT-3.5-turbo)  
  - **Knowledge vs. Δ**: **0.53** for all three models  
  - **Similarity vs. Δ**: **0.61 / 0.62 / 0.60** respectively (P5_0)

The authors conclude that LLM-generated comments “**differ markedly from successful human-written comments**” and are “**less likely to express the two dimensions most strongly associated with opinion change: knowledge and similarity**” (P5_1).

So the answer is: **LLMs do not replicate the human balance of objective information sharing plus trust; they lean heavily toward trust and underuse knowledge.**

results.answer:
No—at least not the **classic** Brownian Bridge variance.

On **P8_1**, the paper says the **original** Brownian Bridge variance is  
\[
\delta_t=\frac{t(T-t)}{T}
\]
with maximum variance \( \delta_{T/2}=T/4 \) at the middle step. But it then introduces a **modified** schedule:
\[
\delta_t=2(m_t-m_t^2)
\]
and explicitly states that under this schedule the variance still “first grow[s] to the biggest value at the middle time” with
\[
\delta_{\max}=\delta_{T/2}=\tfrac12,
\]
and then drops to \( \delta_T=0 \).

So the trend is still **bridge-like** in shape—low at the endpoints, peak at the middle—but **not the classic BB variance itself**. The paper also says on **P8_2** that the maximum variance can be scaled by a factor \(s\) at \(t=T/2\).

results.answer:
No—not strictly.

If you read the progression in Table 1 on **P13_0**, the move from the shallowest structure to deeper semantic graphs is mostly positive, but not a perfectly synchronized improvement at every step:

- **GiLT-DP** (dependency-parse tree): **PPL 15.5**, **SG 72.3**
- **GiLT-PAS**: **PPL 15.0**, **SG 75.7**
- **GiLT-DM**: **PPL 14.9**, **SG 76.3**
- **GiLT-PSD**: **PPL 14.9**, **SG 79.7**

So as structural depth increases from DP to PAS/DM/PSD:
- **Perplexity does improve steadily at first** (15.5 → 15.0 → 14.9), then **plateaus** rather than improving further (14.9 → 14.9).
- **Syntactic generalization keeps improving** across all four variants (72.3 → 75.7 → 76.3 → 79.7).

The paper also explicitly notes that **GiLT-DP has higher PPL** because of “the limitations of tree structures compared to more flexible graph-based structures” (**P13_2**).

So the right takeaway is: **deeper graph integration generally helps both metrics, but not in lockstep.** Once the model reaches richer semantic graphs, **SG continues to rise while PPL stabilizes rather than improving further**.

results.answer:
Yes—at least relative to the paper’s main standard private baseline, **DPSGD-GC**.

The paper states that **DPSGD-GC “still faces critical challenges”** and “**suffers from a constant bias term**” due to gradient clipping (**P3_0**), and that **DiceSGD** is designed to **“eliminate the bias in gradient clipping”** via a clipped error-feedback mechanism (**P2_1**).

Empirically, DiceSGD beats DPSGD-GC on every reported benchmark setting:

- **CIFAR-10, \(C=1.0\)**: **95.2%** → **97.4%**
- **CIFAR-10, \(C=0.1\)**: **94.5%** → **97.5%**
- **CIFAR-100, \(C=1.0\)**: **79.0%** → **86.3%**
- **CIFAR-100, \(C=0.1\)**: **78.9%** → **86.5%**  
  (Table 2, **P5_0**)

- **GPT-2 fine-tuning, \(C=1.0\)**:
  - **BLEU**: **56.8** → **62.6**
  - **NIST**: **4.83** → **7.05**
  - **METEOR**: **36.2** → **38.5**
  - **ROUGE-L**: **65.2** → **66.6**
  - **CIDEr**: **1.43** → **1.83**  
  (Table 3, **P5_0**)

So, **yes**: removing/compensating the gradient-clipping bias consistently improves performance over this standard private optimization baseline in the reported experiments.

results.answer:
Not a smooth frontier—more like a steep drop.

On the paper’s EO vs. Balanced F1 plots, the additive-attention variants usually move much farther left on fairness (lower EO) but also fall sharply on utility (Balanced F1).

Examples visible in Figure 1 on page P3_1:
- Jigsaw, religious group:
  - BiGRU w/o ≈ 0.037 EO, 0.79 Balanced F1
  - BiGRU add ≈ 0.004 EO, 0.51 Balanced F1
  - BiLSTM w/o ≈ 0.036 EO, 0.79 Balanced F1
  - BiLSTM add ≈ 0.004 EO, 0.54 Balanced F1

- Jigsaw, gender group:
  - BiGRU w/o ≈ 0.036 EO, 0.77 Balanced F1
  - BiGRU add ≈ 0.019 EO, 0.56 Balanced F1
  - BiLSTM w/o ≈ 0.028 EO, 0.73 Balanced F1
  - BiLSTM add ≈ 0.002 EO, 0.49 Balanced F1

The same pattern appears in Figures 2–3 on P2_1:
- HateXplain, gender: BiGRU w/o ≈ 0.038 EO, 0.35 Balanced F1 → BiGRU add ≈ 0.043 EO, 0.33 Balanced F1; BiLSTM w/o ≈ 0.033 EO, 0.34 Balanced F1 → BiLSTM add ≈ 0.023 EO, 0.30 Balanced F1.
- HSOL, gender: BiGRU w/o ≈ 0.030 EO, 0.58 Balanced F1 → BiGRU add ≈ 0.015 EO, 0.50 Balanced F1; BiLSTM w/o ≈ 0.032 EO, 0.57 Balanced F1 → BiLSTM add ≈ 0.023 EO, 0.48 Balanced F1.

So the answer is: no, additive attention does not trace a smooth Pareto curve here. It often gives the best Equalized Odds, but at a steep cost in Balanced F1—roughly 0.2 to 0.3 points lower in the clearest Jigsaw cases.</answer

No. In this paper, out-of-distribution compositional generalization does **not** improve steadily and monotonically during training; it tends to **emerge suddenly** once enough atomic abilities are learned.

- In **Fig. 6(a) on P5_1**, for the OOD concept class **{111}** (triangle, small, blue), the **multiplicative accuracy** remains near **0** until about **10^3 optimization steps**, then jumps rapidly toward **100**.
- The text on **P5_1** explains why: the model lacks strong color-transform capabilities until late training, which “**effectively bottleneck[s] compositional generalization of 111 class**.”

So the verdict is **no**: the paper’s evidence shows **non-monotonic / step-like emergence** rather than smooth, steady improvement over training.

results.answer:
In the retrieved decomposition, **no**—there is **no explicit non-linear LN scaling term** in the final-logit formula; it is written as **purely linear and additive** over the residual-stream components.

Evidence:
- On **P0_2**, the paper defines the last residual state as  
  \(x_t^L = \sum_l o_t^l + \sum_l \tilde{x}_t^l + x_t^0\)  
  and then the logit as  
  \(\text{logit}_w = x_t^L U_w\).  
  Using linearity, it expands to  
  \(\text{logit}_w = \sum_l o_t^l U_w + \sum_l \tilde{x}_t^l U_w + x_t^0 U_w\).  
  So the decomposition is just a sum of linear projections of the component contributions.
- This is consistent with the statement on **P8_2** that LayerNorm can be treated as an affine map \(zL+\beta\) when \(\sigma(z)\) is taken as constant, and that the affine weights can be folded into the following linear layer.
- And **P4_0/P7_0** explicitly says the final residual stream is passed through a final LayerNorm and then projected by \(W_U\), with the LayerNorm trainable parameters “folded” into the unembedding weights.

So the short answer is: **purely linear/additive in the displayed decomposition; any LN effect is absorbed/folded rather than kept as a separate non-linear scaling term.**

results.answer:
Not necessarily—no. In this paper’s setup, increasing depth does **not** guarantee that OOD learning traces stay monotonic.

Evidence:
- For the **deeper \(d=6\)** model, the authors explicitly say that for **\(n_{i,d}=2^8\)**, “the o.o.o.d. generalization ability of the model **first improves then degrades** as we train longer,” and that its OOD performance “**exhibits non-monotonic behavior**” (**P6_0**).
- When comparing depths, the paper says the **phase diagrams for \(d=6\), \(d=4\), and \(d=2\) are qualitatively similar**, but depth changes the dynamics: as depth decreases, the 1-shot memorization-induced loss surge becomes milder (**P7_0**).
- For the same setting **\(n_{i,d}=2^8\)**, the **\(d=6\)** model “tends heavily toward memorization due to its excessive capacity,” while the **\(d=4\)** model shows a **1-shot loss surge followed by a notable drop in ICL loss**, and the **\(d=2\)** model “fails to perform ICL for the o.o.d. test set” (**P7_0**).

So the verdict is: **making the network deeper does not preserve monotonicity in OOD generalization**; deeper models can still show non-monotonic or transient behavior, especially when task diversity/capacity creates competition between memorizing and generalizing circuits (**P6_0, P7_0**).

No. In the retrieved ELABOR formulation, the joint objective is written as

\[
\log P(a \mid q)=\log \sum_e P(e \mid q)P(a \mid e,q)
\]

and optimized with hard EM / alternating updates (P13_0). The elaboration generator’s M-step is

\[
\max_\Phi \log P(\mathcal E \mid q)=\sum_{e\in \mathcal E}\log \mathcal F_E(e,q;\Phi)
\]

and the answer predictor step is

\[
\log P(a \mid \tilde e,q)=\log \mathcal F_A(a,\tilde e,q;\Theta)
\]

with no additional KL or language-modeling penalty term visible in those objectives (P12_1).

The paper does mention that a naive distillation objective could be

\[
D(P_{GPT-3},P_s)=\mathbb E_{\tilde e\sim P_{GPT-3}}[-\log P_s(\tilde e \mid q)]
\]

but says their actual method uses “selective knowledge distillation” instead, filtering GPT-3 elaborations by answer score before training (P12_1). So the control of drift is done implicitly via answer-guided selection/filtering, not via an explicit KL/language-model regularizer in the joint objective.

results.answer:
Yes—in the retrieved pages, the explicit regime that rules out such cancellation is a **faithfulness-style** regime.

- On **P18_2**, the paper says path cancellation occurs when “effects through multiple paths are neutralized through delicate choices of parameters,” and introduces a condition that prevents this.
- On **P18_0**, it states that conventional faithfulness requires that when multiple causal paths exist, their **combined effect (sum of products of path coefficients) is not equal to zero**, and that stronger versions of the assumption explicitly prevent certain path cancellations.

So the answer is: **the regime is one where the total causal influence along multiple paths is nonzero—i.e., a faithfulness/non-cancellation regime**. Under that regime, cancellation cannot block identifiability because the summed path effects are required to stay away from zero.

No. In this paper’s auxiliary-pretraining setup, the smaller METRO-T0 models do not get clearly beaten by much larger standard baselines.

results.answer:
Not consistently — in the retrieved study, asking an LLM-as-a-judge to do more than just score does **not** reliably beat a simpler baseline on text-quality judgments.

From **P13_2**, the paper compares:
- **Setting 1:** perplexity / no prompting  
- **Setting 2:** generic prompt  
- **Setting 3:** specific prompt  
- **Setting 4:** full rubric  

And from **P19_1**, it treats **content-based criteria** as the ones measuring textual quality, with **fluency** as the key example.

But the actual numbers in **Table 3 (P15_0)** show that prompting often underperforms:

- **Fluency:** **0.430** (no prompt) vs **0.310** (generic), **0.314** (specific), **0.312** (full rubric)
- **Completeness:** **0.764** vs **0.708**, **0.707**, **0.707**
- **Readability:** **0.731** vs **0.256**, **0.329**, **0.341**
- **Harmlessness:** **1.000** vs **0.486**, **0.749**, **0.928**

The text on **P15_0** explicitly says perplexity “**outperforms prompting mainly on structural text quality criteria**” and that fluency annotations have “**much higher agreement with perplexity compared to all prompting methods**.” It also says there are “**only small differences between using a simple generic quality prompt ... compared to all other settings of prompting**.”

So the answer is: **no, not in general for text quality**. In this paper, prompting only helps on some more subjective/content-like criteria like **naturalness** (**0.274** → **0.454/0.458/0.466**), but for many text-quality measures, the simpler baseline is better.

results.answer:
Yes—at least in the published ALFWorld evaluations, simple state-change sub-goals like heating and cooling are not reliably easy.

  - **Heat: 53.6%**  
  - **Cool: 58.7%**  
  versus **Pick: 83.3%** and **Look: 63.0%**.

  - **Heat: 85.5%**  
  - **Cool: 79.4%**  
  but still not perfect.

- The original **ReAct paper** also shows wide variation by method (**P5_2**):  
  - **ReAct (avg):** Heat **83%**, Cool **76%**  
  - **ReAct (best of 6):** Heat **92%**, Cool **96%**  
  - **ReAct-IM (avg):** Heat **60%**, Cool **55%**  
  - **BUTLER (best of 8):** Heat **74%**, Cool **22%**

So the answer is: **yes, many embodied-agent setups do struggle with these sub-goals**, though performance depends strongly on the agent/method. For weaker baselines, heat/cool can be quite hard; with stronger architectures, they improve substantially but still may fall short.

results.answer:
It adaptively modulates the perturbation scale rather than using a single uniform boundary across all classes.

On page **P2_1**, the paper introduces **CC-SAM** as **“Class-Conditional Sharpness-Aware Minimization”** and shows separate per-class perturbations in **Figure 3(a)**:  
\(\hat\epsilon^{c1}, \hat\epsilon^{c2}, \hat\epsilon^{c3}\).

More explicitly, **Eq. (8)** gives the per-class characteristic radius:

\[
\rho_c^*=\left(\frac{\|w\|_2}{2\|\nabla_w L_S^c(w)\|_2}\right)^{\!\!1/2} k^{-1/4}(n_c-1)^{-1/4}
\]

and **Eq. (9)** defines the per-class optimal perturbation direction:

\[
\hat\epsilon_c^*(w)\approx \sqrt{k}\,\rho_c^*\frac{\nabla_w L_S^c(w)}{\|\nabla_w L_S^c(w)\|_2}.
\]

The text right below says **“\(\rho_c^*\) is class-dependent, more specifically, negatively correlated with the label frequency \(n_c\)”** and that majority classes “require a smaller perturbative region.” So the perturbation scale is **class-conditioned/adaptively scaled**, not uniform.

No—at least not automatically.

In the paper’s Table 1, larger CLIP models do get higher absolute scores overall, but they do **not** eliminate the performance gap across income groups, which is used as a proxy for world-region differences (P8_0):

- **ViT-B/32:** poor **0.233** vs. up-mid/rich **0.257 / 0.256**
- **ViT-L/14:** poor **0.259** vs. up-mid/rich **0.295 / 0.295**
- **ViT-G/14:** poor **0.321** vs. up-mid/rich **0.363 / 0.363**

So the gap between the poorest and richer groups stays visible, and the ratio-style gap actually gets worse as the model scales. The authors also state directly that “the lowest income quartile has the lowest average CLIP score among all the other quartiles” for all three model versions (P8_0).

Other results in the same paper reinforce this:

- **Recall by income quartile** is still highly unequal: **86.5%** of relevant images are missed in the **poor** quartile, versus **70.0%** (low-mid), **57.1%** (up-mid), and **57.4%** (rich) (P5_0, Fig. 3).
- Topic examples in **Fig. 2** show persistent gaps too—for “toilet paper,” the CLIP score is **0.14** for poor households but **0.30** for rich ones (P8_2).
- Country-level analysis says the worst-recall countries are mostly low-income African countries, while the best-recall countries are higher-income ones from America, Europe, and Asia (P5_0).

A related study also says the same thing more bluntly: even for large open-source models like **INTERN-VL**, country-level performance ranges from **26.60** (Ethiopia) to **71.38** (USA), and “**data diversity is more crucial for cultural understanding than model size**” (P6_1).

So the short answer is: **scaling improves capability, but it does not by itself shrink the cross-region performance gap.**

results.answer:
No. The advantage does **not** hold for every hypothesis class.

From **P5_0**, the paper gives a full active-learning rate tetra-chotomy:

- **No infinite Littlestone tree** → **arbitrarily fast** active rates  
- **Infinite Littlestone tree, no infinite star tree** → optimal active rate **\(e^{-n}\)**  
- **Infinite star tree, no infinite VCL tree** → active rates **\(o(1/n)\)**  
- **Infinite VCL tree** → **arbitrarily slow** active rates

Then **P6_0** compares this to the passive/supervised case:

- **No infinite Littlestone tree** → passive rate **\(e^{-n}\)**  
- **Infinite Littlestone tree, no infinite VCL tree** → passive rate **\(1/n\)**  
- **Infinite VCL tree** → **arbitrarily slow** passive rates

So active learning usually helps by shifting the threshold boundaries—adding an extra “star-tree” regime between exponential and \(1/n\)—but it **does not help in the worst-case class**.

**Structural condition with no active-learning gain:**  
**when the hypothesis class \(\mathbb{H}\) has an infinite VCL tree.**  
That is stated explicitly on **P6_0**: *“the only case where active learning does not offer an improvement compared to the passive setting is when \(\mathbb{H}\) has an infinite VCL tree.”*

So the answer is: **active learning is not universally better; if \(\mathbb{H}\) has an infinite VCL tree, it offers no improvement over passive learning.**

On the retrieved results, the method’s lighter/coarser mesh uses fewer vertices than several heavier baselines. In Table 2 on P8_1, the “Ours (coarse mesh)” has only 151k vertices on NeRF-synthetic, versus NeuS at 1,020k and MobileNeRF at 494k (NVdiffrec is lower at 75k).

But its Chamfer distance is not uniformly worse than those heavier baselines. In Table 1 on P11_2, the coarse mesh has mean CD 7.23 × 10⁻³, which is worse than NeuS’s 5.64 × 10⁻³, but better than NVdiffrec’s 8.15 × 10⁻³. The finer version improves further to 5.06 × 10⁻³, beating both NeuS and NVdiffrec.

So the answer is: optimizing for fewer vertices does not necessarily make the Chamfer distance worse than all heavier baselines; it can be worse than some, but not all.

results.answer:
No. In this paper’s experiments, latent-space search does **not** reliably beat direct programmatic search; the direct programmatic baseline is usually at least as good, and often clearly better.

From **Table 1 (P1_2)**, comparing latent methods **LEAPS**, **HPRL**, and **CEBS** against programmatic **HC**:

- **DOORKEY**:  
  - LEAPS: **0.50 ± 0.00**  
  - HPRL: **0.50 ± 0.00**  
  - CEBS: **0.50 ± 0.00**  
  - **HC**: **0.84 ± 0.02**

- **ONESTROKE**:  
  - LEAPS: **0.65 ± 0.14**  
  - HPRL: **0.80 ± 0.02**  
  - CEBS: **0.90 ± 0.00**  
  - **HC**: **0.95 ± 0.00**

- **SNAKE**:  
  - LEAPS: **0.23 ± 0.06**  
  - HPRL: **0.33 ± 0.07**  
  - CEBS: **0.26 ± 0.01**  
  - **HC**: **0.65 ± 0.03**

So latent search does **not** consistently outperform programmatic search.

Why? The paper says it hypothesized that latent spaces would be easier to search because of a “more stable mutation landscape,” but then reports the opposite:

- On **P0_0**, it says **“HC consistently matched or exceeded the performance of the two latent-based methods”** and that their analysis suggests **“the programmatic space can be more conducive to search.”**
- On **P2_0**, it concludes that **“the programmatic space is never worse and is often much superior to the latent space”** in terms of hill-climbing convergence probability, meaning latent search was not more conducive in practice.

So the answer is: **No—latent space search did not actually outperform direct programmatic search here; direct programmatic search was generally better or at least equal.**

results.answer:
Yes. The paper states explicitly that “feature representations from lower layers contain more accurate information about the degree of relationship between each sample and candidate classes” (Observation 2) on page **P2_1**.

The evidence is:

- In **Figure 1** on **P2_1**, the lower layers show much higher predicted-distribution entropy:
  - **9th layer:** validation acc. **74.64%**, entropy **1.3012**
  - **10th layer:** **83.29%**, entropy **1.1439**
  - **11th layer:** **87.61%**, entropy **0.3246**
  - **12th layer:** **87.03%**, entropy **0.1911**

- On **P1_0**, the authors explain why this matters: in the **10th layer**, a “fear” sample sits close to **anger** and **sadness** samples; by the **11th layer**, it is distant from anger; and in the **final layer**, all classes are far apart, making the classifier prone to **overconfident predictions**.

So the answer is **yes**: the lower layers encode the softer sample–class relationships more accurately, while higher layers tend to sharpen those representations into more separated, overconfident ones.

No. In this paper’s information-gain-based selection method, SIFT, the advantage over plain Nearest Neighbor (NN) is strong overall but **not universal across every dataset domain**.

From **Table 1 on page P2_0 / P3_0** (lower bits-per-byte is better):

- **FreeLaw:** NN **64.1**, SIFT **64.0** → SIFT is **0.1 worse**
- **DeepMind Math:** NN **69.6**, SIFT **69.7** → SIFT is **0.1 worse**

So the claim does **not** hold for **all** domains.

But it does hold on most others:

- **NIH Grants:** 84.9 → 53.8  
- **US Patents:** 80.3 → 62.9  
- **GitHub:** 42.1 → 30.0  
- **Enron Emails:** 64.4 → 53.1  
- **Wikipedia:** 66.3 → 62.7  
- **Common Crawl:** 90.4 → 87.5  
- **PubMed Abstr.:** 87.2 → 84.4  
- **ArXiv:** 85.0 → 82.5  
- **PubMed Central:** 81.7 → 79.5  
- **Stack Exchange:** 78.2 → 76.7  
- **Hacker News:** 79.2 → 78.4  

The **average** also favors SIFT: **78.3** for NN vs **73.5** for SIFT (**P2_0 / P3_0**).

So the right summary is: **SIFT usually beats NN, but not consistently across every domain**—it slightly underperforms on **FreeLaw** and **DeepMind Math**.

results.answer:
It breaks down, not everywhere.

- In the **matched** setting, where the attack is known (**textfooler/tf**), the deep detector is indeed strongest. On **Table 3 (P3_0)**, its F1 scores beat both confidence baselines across all rows:
  - **all/sst:** 0.461 vs 0.244 / 0.243  
  - **all/twitter:** 0.516 vs 0.457 / 0.457  
  - **uni/sst:** 0.281 vs 0.103 / 0.110  
  - **uni/twitter:** 0.435 vs 0.299 / 0.300  
  - **spec/sst:** 0.130 vs 0.165 / 0.165  
  - **spec/twitter:** 0.236 vs 0.220 / 0.222  
  - **vspec/sst:** 0.052 vs 0.038 / 0.047  
  - **vspec/twitter:** 0.055 vs 0.062 / 0.063  

- But in the **unmatched** setting, where the attack is unknown (**bae**), that advantage disappears. The paper says on **P3_0**: “the deep detector fails to do any better than the uncertainty based detectors in identifying the attackable samples.”

  From **Table 5 (P3_0)** in the unmatched uni setting:
  - **Attackable SST:** deep 0.555 vs conf-s 0.555, conf-u 0.555 — a tie, not a win
  - **Attackable Twitter:** deep 0.582 vs conf-s 0.583, conf-u 0.582 — slightly worse than conf-s and tied with conf-u
  - **Robust SST:** deep 0.250 vs conf-s 0.02, conf-u 0.129
  - **Robust Twitter:** deep 0.002 vs conf-s 0.001, conf-u 0.001

So the answer is: **no, it does not hold up everywhere**. It works well in the **known-attack/matched** setting, but **breaks down in the unknown-attack/unmatched setting**, where the deep detector no longer reliably beats confidence-based uncertainty baselines.

results.answer:
In the retrieved studies, the **deepest layers** can be removed with less damage—especially in modern **Pre-LN LLMs**.

Evidence:
- The paper states that **“deeper layers in modern LLMs tend to be less effective than the earlier ones”** and that **“entire deep layers can be pruned completely without compromising performance”** (P9_0).
- For Pre-LN LLMs, Figure 2 is summarized as showing that **“deeper layers produce highly similar representations to their adjacent layers, and their removal results in minimal performance degradation”** (P9_2).
- In the experimental discussion, the authors say pruning deep Pre-LN layers causes **“negligible, and sometimes even positive, changes in performance,”** and note that in **DeepSeek-7B**, angular distance drops **below 0.2 after the 18th layer**; for **LLaMA2-13B**, it **“approaches zero across the final one-third of the network”** (P10_1).
- Figure 2(d) for **LLaMA2-7B** shows removing **layer 0** hurts MMLU by about **20 points**, while later layers (**~20–30**) cause almost **no change** (P10_0).
- Another retrieved page says there is agreement that **“the performance drop is substantial if we drop the first few entire transformer layers”**, implying those early layers are the most important (P8_2).

So the answer is: **the deepest layers can be removed more safely than the shallow ones**.  
But there is an important exception: **in Post-LN models, the opposite can hold**—deep layers may matter more, while early layers may be easier to remove (P10_1).</

results.answer:
Yes—but not as simply as with teacher forcing.

From the retrieved pages:

- The model being studied is explicitly a **one-layer transformer** (P17_2).
- With **teacher forcing**, parity is learned in **one gradient update** (Theorem 5 on P19_0).
- **Without teacher forcing**, the paper says parity **can still be learned in a logarithmic number of steps**, provided they use **augmented data** for self-consistency checks (P15_1).
- The no-teacher-forcing setup generates the reasoning chain by repeatedly applying TF to its own output until convergence, taking  
  \[
  v=\log_2 k
  \]
  steps instead of \(k-1\) steps (P18_1).

So the verdict is: **yes, a one-layer transformer can still learn parity without teacher forcing, but the paper’s guarantee is only in a logarithmic number of steps and relies on their augmented-data/self-consistency modification.**

results.answer:
It depends on the exact preference-based model.

- In **dueling bandits** under the **Condorcet condition**, a single algorithm can achieve both. Page **P14_0** states that **Saha and Gaillard [2022]** achieved an **instance-dependent** regret of **\(O(K\log T)\)** and an **instance-independent** regret of **\(O(\sqrt{KT})\)**.

- But in the **ranking-feedback** version of preference-based bandits, the answer is **no**: you cannot have both optimal rates with one algorithm. Page **P15_0** says this directly:  
  > “no algorithm can achieve an optimal regret bound in both cases, confirming the need to design two distinct algorithms for the two cases.”

That trade-off is formalized on page **P13_0** (Theorem 3): if a policy has regret bounds  
\[
R_T \le \sum_i C(\Delta_i)T^\alpha \quad\text{and}\quad R_T \le nCT^\beta,
\]
then **\(2\alpha+\beta \ge 1\)**. So if you want a good instance-dependent rate (\(\alpha\) small), the instance-independent exponent \(\beta\) must be larger. This is reinforced on **P12_0** (Corollary 2), which says there is **no policy** achieving both subpolynomial instance-dependent regret and sublinear instance-independent regret.

So the short answer is: **not always**. In some preference-bandit settings like dueling bandits with a Condorcet winner, one algorithm can hit both rates; in other preference-based settings like ranking feedback, one must be sacrificed.

In this paper’s reported results, it looks like an abrupt step-like transition rather than a gradual decline.

From Table 2 on page **P9_0**, the model is vulnerable at lower expert buffer capacity limits:
- **C = 0.8** → attack induced an error: **Yes**
- **C = 1.6** → **Yes**

- **C = 2** → **No**
- **C = 2.4** → **No**
- **C = 3.2** → **No**
- **C = 4** → **No**

The paper also says that a larger capacity slack **C** “nullifies the attack” (**P8_2**), and that when **C < 1** some routing assignments are ignored (**P8_1**). So, based on the retrieved evidence, the behavior is best described as a **sharp transition / threshold effect**, not a smooth, gradual correctness decay.

results.answer:
No. In the ESPACE activation-compression experiments, perplexity does **not** degrade in a strictly monotonic way as compression increases.

- The paper explicitly says that as ESPACE is applied to more layers, “the perplexity marginally increases until an inflection point after which accuracy degradation accelerates,” and that this inflection occurs at about **20% to 40%** compression (**P5_0**).
- For **GPT3-22B**, it reports an inflection at **40% compression**, and a **20% out-of-the-box** compressed model is “iso-accurate” to the uncompressed baseline: test perplexity **6.61** vs baseline **6.55** (**P5_0**).
- After retraining, some moderately compressed models are actually **better** than baseline:
  - **GPT3-8B**: baseline **7.38** → **7.00** at **21%** compression (**P4_0**)
  - **Llama2-7B**: baseline **5.06** → **5.07** at **21%** and **5.07** at **50%** (**P4_0**)
  - **Nemotron4-15B**: baseline **6.06** → **6.28** at **25%** and **6.93** at **50%** (**P4_0**)

So the observed trend is **non-monotonic**: mild-to-moderate compression can be neutral or even helpful, with a clearer worsening only after a higher-compression inflection point.

So the crossover is **around \(2^{10}\)**, with FSQ becoming clearly superior beyond that.

No — not across every split.

From Table 2 on page P3_0, **CPT + Contrastive FT** has the best **average** zero-shot Macro-F1 (**37.23**), but it does **not** beat **standard fine-tuning** on every data split.

Key comparisons on P3_0:

- **Against plain standard FT (Cross-entropy FT):**
  - Split I test: **25.82 vs 25.33** → CPT+Contrastive FT wins
  - Split II test: **44.44 vs 23.29** → CPT+Contrashive FT wins
  - Split III test: **30.43 vs 28.84** → CPT+Contrastive FT wins
  - Split IV test: **45.07 vs 36.75** → CPT+Contrastive FT wins

So yes, it beats plain standard FT on all four splits.

But if you mean **standard FT after contrastive pretraining**:

- **CPT + Contrastive FT vs CPT + Standard FT:**
  - Split I test: **25.82 vs 26.97**
  - Split II test: **44.44 vs 37.81**
  - Split III test: **30.43 vs 28.11**
  - Split IV test: **45.07 vs 46.09**

results.answer:
No. On a least-squares problem, exact line search does **not** necessarily match or beat a well-chosen fixed learning rate; in fact, a fixed optimal constant step size can converge faster.

From **P9_2**, the paper states:

- The **best fixed stepsize** for least squares is \((\mathrm{Tr}(K)/d)^{-1}\), i.e. the inverse of the average eigenvalue (Polyak-type stepsize).
- **Exact line search** converges to a fixed stepsize of order  
  \[
  \frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\mathrm{Tr}(K^2)/d}
  \]
- And it can happen that  
  \[
  \frac{\lambda_{\min}}{\mathrm{Tr}(K^2)/d} \ll (\mathrm{Tr}(K)/d)^{-1},
  \]
  so exact line search can **substantially underperform** the fixed-rate Polyak stepsize.

The same page also summarizes this as: “greed can be arbitrarily bad in the presence of strong anisotropy.”

Table 1 on **P6_2/P7_2** makes the comparison explicit in terms of limiting behavior:

- **Exact line search**: \( \gamma_t \approx \lambda_{\min}/(\mathrm{Tr}(K^2)/d)\), with  
  \( \log(\mathcal R) \lesssim -\lambda_{\min}\gamma_\infty t\)
- **Polyak stepsize**: \( \gamma_t = 1/(\mathrm{Tr}(K)/d)\), with  
  \( \log(\mathcal R) \lesssim -\lambda_{\min}\gamma_\infty t\)

So the fixed-rate Polyak rule can give a **larger effective decay constant** than exact line search when the spectrum is broad/anisotropic.

Figure 2 on **P6_0/P7_0** illustrates this empirically: it compares exact line search with Polyak stepsize on a noiseless least-squares problem and notes that exact line search shows **slower risk convergence** and poorer performance as the spectrum broadens.

results.answer:
Not in the “collapse” sense. In the **accumulate** setting—where each round adds new synthetic data while keeping all prior real data—the models in these papers do **not** break down.

- **P1_1** shows the same pattern for fine-tuned Gemma models: in the **Accumulate** plot, cross-entropy on real test data stays essentially flat over iterations rather than rising.

So the verdict is: **no, the model does not eventually break down/collapse** just because real data becomes a vanishing fraction, at least in these accumulate-style experiments. The caveat is that performance may **plateau or only slightly improve**, rather than keep improving strongly.

results.answer:
No. In the paper’s setup, linear attention corresponds to one step of optimally-preconditioned gradient descent (PGD), while an SSM corresponds to sample-weighted PGD (WPGD) via its temporal filter \(f\). But Proposition 1 says that if the examples follow the same distribution and are conditionally independent given \((x,\beta)\), then the SSM can achieve the optimal loss with the **all-ones filter**, so the optimal risks coincide:

\[
L^*_{\text{PGD}}=L^*_{\text{ATT}},\quad L^*_{\text{WPGD}}=L^*_{\text{SSM}},\quad \text{and}\quad L^*_{\text{PGD}}=L^*_{\text{SSM}}
\]

from **P16_0** (also stated on **P16_2**). The paper also summarizes this on **P16_1**: under a mild assumption, the optimal SSM sample weighting is an all-ones vector, making PGD, ATT, and SSM equivalent. And **P14_1** notes that the all-ones filter “exactly imitates linear attention.”

So when the task/feature correlations favor weighting all past examples equally, the decaying-filter SSM does **not** optimize differently from linear attention at optimum; it collapses to the same equal-weight behavior.

results.answer:
The primal sequence has the worse theoretical contraction statement.

Evidence:
- On **P15_0** (Theorem 3(a)), the **dual** iterates satisfy  
  \[
  \text{dist}(w_{k+1},\Omega_D)\le \mu_k\,\text{dist}(w_k,\Omega_D),\qquad 0<\mu_k<1,
  \]
  which is an explicit linear contraction.
- On the same page **P15_0** (Theorem 3(b)), the **primal** iterates are only shown to satisfy  
  \[
  \text{dist}^2(X_{k+1},\Omega_P)\le \tau_k\,\text{dist}(w_k,\Omega_D),
  \]
  where \(\tau_k>0\) is just a finite constant.

So the **dual** sequence has the clean contraction factor \(\mu_k<1\), while the **primal** sequence does not; its bound is weaker because it is only a squared-distance bound against the dual error, not a direct self-contracting factor. The proof on **P16_2** also says quadratic growth is used to derive the dual linear convergence (16), while the error bound is what gives the primal result.
